1: Welcome to Lab manual P fifteen and sixteen, Module three: data quality engineering and anomaly management. In this lab we run every lecture topic, accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, integration, duplicates, encoding, validation rules and scaling, on a real dataset, with the code and the output.
2: Here is the lab roadmap, from a messy merged file to a validated, scaled dataset. Twelve steps. One, audit: shape, types, missing values, duplicate rows and columns. Two, accuracy: present and valid, but believable? Three, completeness: how much is missing and why. Four, consistency: one fact, one spelling. Five, validity: range, set and format rules, then re audit. Six, integration: key, schema, conflicts, duplicates. Seven, duplicates: detect exact, key based and near duplicates. Eight, removal: drop duplicate rows and columns. Nine, encoding: standardise categories and re audit. Ten, validation: one reusable rule table. Eleven, scale: log one p for skew, then standard scaler. Twelve, a second dataset: the same code on Online Shoppers.
3: Two real C S V files, one set of code. The primary lab file is a two source merge of New York Airbnb listings with forty nine thousand eight hundred ninety five rows and seventeen columns. Source A, from Analytics, is the real Inside Airbnb file with forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five listings and a price column. Source B, from Finance, is a thousand of the same listings carrying their own price U S D field. Three hundred of them were exported with lowercase borough and room type, and seven hundred as exact copies. The two exports were concatenated, the way two teams' files often land in one pipeline. Everything else, missing values, skew and ten thousand dollar prices, is genuine. The worked second example is Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention, twelve thousand three hundred thirty rows and eighteen columns.
4: Setup. We import pandas, numpy, matplotlib and standard scaler, then read the merged C S V and look at the first five rows. The columns are I D, name, host I D, host name, neighbourhood group, neighbourhood, latitude, longitude, room type, price, minimum nights, number of reviews, last review, reviews per month, host listings count, availability, and price U S D.
5: Part one: the data quality audit. Profile first, with five commands over the whole dataset and no loops. The shape is forty nine thousand eight hundred ninety five rows by seventeen columns. The total number of missing cells, df dot isnull dot sum dot sum, is twenty thousand five hundred seventy three. Df dot duplicated dot sum counts exact duplicate rows: seven hundred. Df dot T dot duplicated dot sum counts exact duplicate columns: one. And df dot columns of the duplicated transpose tells us which column repeats: price U S D.
6: One table gives the type, gaps and distinct values of every column. We build an audit data frame from dtypes, the missing count, the missing percentage and the number of unique values. Look at neighbourhood group: only five real boroughs, but ten distinct labels. And room type: three real types, but six labels. The audit already exposes a consistency problem.
7: Part two, dimension one: accuracy. Accuracy needs a reference, so we compare each price with a trusted reference, its peers. Our proxy is the median price of listings with the same borough and room type, computed with group by and transform median, which places the peer median on every row. Then the ratio is price divided by peer median, and we sort descending. The top rows are absurd: a private room in Queens at ten thousand dollars versus a peer median of fifty nine, and a private room in Brooklyn at seventy five hundred versus sixty five.
8: Flag suspicious values, but do not delete them yet. Eleven listings are priced at zero dollars a night. Sixty six are priced above twenty times their peer median. And fourteen have a minimum stay longer than a year. Why flag instead of delete? The true price is unknown, and deleting real listings biases the data. So record the suspicion, for example in a price suspect column, and decide on capping or removal in the outlier session, lectures nineteen and twenty.
9: Part three, dimension two: completeness. How much is missing, column by column? Reviews per month and last review are each missing in twenty point five eight percent of rows, host name point zero four percent, and name point zero three percent. At the row level, df dot notnull dot all across axis one, mean times one hundred, shows that seventy nine point three eight percent of rows have no gap at all.
10: Why is last review missing? Check the reason. A cross tab of number of reviews equal to zero against last review being null shows a perfect split. Listings with reviews, thirty nine thousand six hundred twenty seven, all have a last review date. Listings with zero reviews, ten thousand two hundred sixty eight, all have it missing. So twenty point six percent of listings have simply never been reviewed. This is structural, not random: a listing with no reviews cannot have a last review date. The correct fill, in lectures seventeen and eighteen, is reviews per month equals zero, not the column mean.
11: Part four, dimension three: consistency. Across rows, one borough has two spellings. Value counts on neighbourhood group shows ten labels for five real boroughs. Manhattan has twenty one thousand nine hundred eighty five rows, but there is also a lowercase manhattan with one hundred thirty one. Brooklyn and lowercase brooklyn, queens, bronx and staten island all appear twice. A group by on this column would produce ten groups instead of five.
12: Consistency across columns, related fields and sources. Across columns, df of price equals price U S D returns true, the same fact stored twice. Across related fields, a rule that number of reviews equal to zero must match last review being null breaks for zero rows, so it holds. And across sources, the listing with I D thirty five million six hundred fifty one thousand nine hundred eighty two shows Manhattan and Private room in one source and lowercase manhattan and private room in the other.
13: Part five, dimension four: validity. Write the rules first, then test every row against every rule. Price at least zero, minimum nights at least one, latitude and longitude inside New York's bounding box, availability between zero and three sixty five, room type in the allowed set, and borough in the allowed set. The tilde operator flips the table, so counting failures per rule is simple. Failures: price zero, minimum nights zero, latitude five, longitude zero, availability zero, room type three hundred, borough three hundred. In all, three hundred five rows fail at least one rule.
14: Validity versus accuracy: a value can pass one check and fail the other. A private room at ten thousand dollars passes validity, but it is wrong, failing accuracy. A latitude of forty point four nine nine eight, in Staten Island, fails the bounding box rule but is a real place. And lowercase brooklyn is not in the allowed set, but it is the right borough. Validity asks, is this possible, and is checked against a rule. Accuracy asks, is this correct, and is checked against reality. The ten thousand dollar listings pass every validity rule, so validity alone cannot catch them. And the five latitude failures are real listings in Staten Island and Riverdale, so rules need review too.
15: Part six: integration logic. Four steps: match a shared key, align the schemas, resolve conflicts, and re audit. First split the merged table back into source A and source B. Check that every I D in B is found in A, a hundred percent. Then compare the column sets: only A has price, and only B has price U S D. Rename price U S D to price in B, and the schemas are identical. Source A has forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five rows by sixteen columns and B has one thousand by sixteen.
16: Steps three and four: merge on the key, find conflicts and re audit. An outer merge on I D with an indicator shows forty seven thousand eight hundred ninety five rows only in A, one thousand in both, and none only in B. The conflicts are three hundred in borough, three hundred in room type, and zero in price. The conflicts are case only, so the resolution is to keep source A's spelling. The result is forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five rows with zero duplicates.
17: Part seven: duplicate detection. Three kinds. Exact duplicates: every column identical, seven hundred rows. Same key duplicates: the I D appears more than once, one thousand rows, which are the seven hundred copies plus the three hundred lowercase rows. And near duplicates: lowercase and trim the name, collapse repeated spaces, then compare with the same host. That finds four hundred eighty one candidates, which you review and never delete automatically.
18: Part eight: duplicate removal. Rows and columns need two different one line fixes. For rows, df dot drop duplicates keeps the first copy. For columns, take the transpose duplicated flags, and keep the non duplicate columns with the tilde operator. Before and after: rows go from forty nine thousand eight hundred ninety five to forty nine thousand one hundred ninety five, and columns from seventeen to sixteen, dropping price U S D. Notice three hundred repeated I Ds remain, because the lowercase copies are not yet exact duplicates.
19: Part nine: inconsistent encoding. Standardise categories across the whole column at once. Strip and title case the borough, strip and capitalise the room type, and strip and collapse spaces in the name. The number of distinct borough labels goes from ten to five, and room type from six to three. For messy codes, use a mapping with replace, for example B K and Bklyn both become Brooklyn.
20: Re audit after every fix. Standardising created three hundred new exact duplicates. Lowercase brooklyn does not equal Brooklyn, so it hid three hundred copies from drop duplicates. After title casing they became exact duplicates, so the audit must run again after each cleaning step. Dropping them gives forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five rows by sixteen columns, the true unique listings, identical to the correctly integrated table from part six. Manhattan has twenty one thousand six hundred sixty one rows, Brooklyn twenty thousand one hundred four, and Queens five thousand six hundred sixty six.
21: Part ten: data validation rules. One reusable rule table, to re run on every load. A range rule: price is at least zero. A type rule: price is an integer. A uniqueness rule: I D is unique. A set rule: room type is in the allowed set. After cleaning, all twelve rules pass, including price at least zero, minimum nights at least one, availability between zero and three sixty five, last review is a date, I D is unique, no duplicate rows, no duplicate columns, room type in set, and borough in set.
22: Part eleven, standardisation and scale. Step one: measure skew for every numeric column at once with df of num cols dot skew. Then log all skewed columns in one line with numpy log one p, add a log suffix, and join them back. Skewness raw versus after log one p: price falls from nineteen point one two to point five five, minimum nights from twenty one point eight three to three point one three, number of reviews from about seven point nine three to point three six, reviews per month and host listings also fall sharply.
23: Log one p tames the long right tail of price. On the left, price in dollars has skew nineteen point one two, with almost everything crammed to the left. On the right, log one p of price has skew point five five, a nearly bell shaped distribution. The code is price log equals numpy log one p of price. Log of one plus x is safe for the eleven zero dollar prices, because log of zero would be undefined.
24: Step two: standard scaler puts every feature on one scale. The z score is x minus mean divided by standard deviation. Fit transform on the chosen columns, wrap the result in a data frame, add a z suffix, and join. Price had a mean of one fifty two point seven and a standard deviation of two forty before. After scaling, every z column has a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. Do not scale identifiers and coordinates, I D, host I D, latitude and longitude. And log first, then scale, so outliers do not set the new mean and standard deviation.
25: Part twelve: the final re audit, the whole lab in one table. Rows go from forty nine thousand eight hundred ninety five to forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five. Original columns kept go from seventeen to sixteen. Duplicate rows go from seven hundred to zero, duplicate columns from one to zero, repeated I Ds from one thousand to zero. Borough labels go from ten to five and room type labels from six to three. Price skew falls to point five five after the log. And twelve of twelve validation rules pass. The cleaned file is saved for lectures seventeen and eighteen, with twenty eight columns. Still open are the missing values, and the flagged zero and ten thousand dollar prices.
26: Part thirteen: the same code on a second dataset, Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention. Twelve thousand three hundred thirty rows by eighteen columns, zero missing cells, one hundred twenty five duplicate rows, and zero duplicate columns. Two findings. Consistency: nine months use three letter codes, but June is spelled out. Completeness: there are zero empty cells, yet January and April never appear, so coverage gaps count too. The encoding fix is to replace June with Jun.
27: Validity, accuracy, duplicates and scale on Online Shoppers. Validity rules have zero failures. For accuracy, twenty two sessions spent more than four hours on products, with a maximum of seventeen point eight hours, so check them. Zero rows have no pages but positive time. After drop duplicates, twelve thousand two hundred five rows remain. And a warning on the log: the product related duration skew goes from seven point two five to minus one point four three, so log one p can over correct. Re check skew after every transform.
28: Key takeaways. Audit first, with shape, isnull sum, duplicated sum and T duplicated sum. Validity is checked against rules and accuracy against reality, and the ten thousand dollar room passes every rule. Completeness includes why data is missing, and which categories never appear. Integrate on a key, align schemas, resolve conflicts, then re audit. Standardising labels can create new duplicates, so re run the audit after every fix. And log one p first, standard scaler second: skew falls from nineteen point one two to point five five, and every feature is at mean zero and standard deviation one. The same audit works on any dataset.
